a number of respected researchers (e.g. @DKokotajlo @bshlgrs @ajeya_cotra @RyanGreenblatt)  have suggested that the METR-documented ~2x speedup in AI progress at anthropic over the last year supports the hypothesis that there will be a near-term (e.g. 2027) intelligence explosion (IE). how exactly does this reasoning work?

one way to think about this: perhaps the leading alternative to the near-term IE hypothesis is what we might call the factor F hypothesis, which says that there's at least one key factor F [e.g. creativity, research vision, planning ability, ...] such that (i) high F is required for an AI system to reach the superhuman levels required for full-scale IE [e.g. ASI, artificial superhuman general intelligence or at least SAR, superhuman AI researcher], and (ii) F is so difficult to build into AI systems that leading AI systems won't have high F in the near term. i don't know whether the factor F hypothesis is true, but it's not obvious to me why the 2x speedup makes it much less likely. 

it's widely agreed that the 2x speedup reflects an even larger (perhaps 10x) speedup in other capacities G such as coding and experimentation.  under the F hypothesis, G could explode locally, leading to major progress in sub-AGI capacities without much progress in F (think of G as the easy part of AGI and F as the hard part). that tends to lead just to a weak form of recursive self-improvement (call it an intelligence subexplosion) below AGI levels.

the AI futures document responding to the METR report is usefully explicit about nearby issues. the authors report believing in a high-ish growth rate for "research taste" (AI research factors beyond coding and experimentation) relative to increases in general capacity. presumably they take potential Fs to be aspects of research taste that will grow fast too. but i don't really see where the evidence counts again a relatively-low-growth F hypothesis where F stays below threshold for years.  maybe one could argue that the explosion in G provides bayesian evidence against this F hypothesis (G's exploding is antecedently less likely under the F hypothesis than under its negation), but that's far from clear, and even if true there will remain a solid mass of credence under the F hypothesis.

maybe there are other reasons to reject the factor F hypothesis: e.g. because AI research is relevantly like math research, and AI math research is becoming superhuman already. but if we have reasons like that, the 2x speedup isn't really needed to make the case for near-term SAR and IE. maybe the 2x speedup could speed up an expected IE slightly from 2028 (two years away) to 2027 (one year away), and/or maybe it could be extrapolated into ever-faster speedups (another 2x in 6 months, 3 months, and so on) converging in 2027. but those are very different arguments that require huge premises to work. 

am i missing something here?  i'm curious to hear which evidential routes from 2x speedup to near-term IE people have in mind. 

N.B. i'm not saying you shouldn't worry about near-term ASI. i'm worried!

And there’s also some real chance that AI takeover is basically fine or good. I think you should think of this as similar to what happens when a technologically advanced civilization runs across a less technologically sophisticated one, e.g. when the Europeans colonized the Americas or Australia. The colonizers sometimes engage in brutal violence and sometimes don’t. I don’t know what will happen. There’s also a possibility that the AIs secretly take over and humans don’t find out about it for a few years. I also think that there is a pretty high chance of weirder outcomes that are also extremely scary. (If you want to read more about what happens to people in the event of AI takeover, you can read this, but note that it’s pretty weird and not aimed at a general audience. https://t.co/F6fGRrcSpa)

Overall, I think there’s a very real possibility (maybe 20%) that within a year, AI misalignment issues prevent you from going about life normally, because you are dead or enslaved or because of collateral damage related to all this (e.g. because bioweapons are released or major wars have started). (Some of this probability comes from those events occurring before superintelligence is developed.)

I am working to try to prevent this, obviously, as I’ve been doing for the last nine years. I am not sure what strategy is best. My best guess is that I should try to slow AI development and also try to reduce the probability that the superintelligent AIs are misaligned if they are produced soon.

Obviously, the claim I'm making here is quite extreme and surprising, and I definitely don't think that I defended my view adequately here. I wrote this quickly and might not endorse some of the details if I think about them more. But it seems better to state what I roughly overall think than to not say anything.

I don’t know what you should do.

I am very sad about this. I have been worried about AI takeover since I was 16, and working to prevent it since I was 23. So some of my emotional processing of all this happened long ago. But the METR report last week (and some related evidence that came out a bit earlier) hit me quite hard. I’m very unhappy that my friends and family and everyone else is at serious risk of being killed pretty soon.

(It feels ridiculous to try to summarize those feelings as “very unhappy”. But the scale of the situation makes it hard to say anything that doesn’t feel like an absurd understatement.)

I am very grateful to all the people who are working to prevent this, and my favorite part of my life is that I’m friends with many brilliant and heroic people who work on this. Unfortunately, I don’t think we’re good enough at our jobs, and I think we’ll probably fail to prevent catastrophe, at least if superintelligence is developed next year. Honestly I am frustrated and sorry that we didn't do a better job of preparing for this.

Baidu just launched ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview, and what it's capable of is pretty incredible.

Take game development, for example. The model built nearly 100 playable mobile games from game design documents.

And no, I'm not talking about simple code demos.

It was given complete game specifications and tasked with building games across different genres, from tower defence and racing to card-based RPGs and interactive stories.

I went through the demo, and a few things caught my eye:

1. It actually builds playable games.

Not just the basic mechanics. It handles the artwork, sound effects, gameplay logic and other pieces needed to make a complete mini-game.

2. It isn't locked into one framework.

That's quite a range.

3. It can test its own games.

This is the part I found particularly interesting.
For most of the games, the model uses simulated players, state-space search and level replays to check whether levels can be completed and whether the gameplay is balanced.
Basically, it doesn't just build something and leave you to figure out what's broken.

4. It pays attention to the little details.

Different games get their own character names, boss dialogues, branching storylines and level names tailored to their genre.

Giving an AI agent access to a wallet is not the difficult part.

The real question is how much freedom should that wallet actually have?

While exploring the MCP setup from @vangrid_io I found an interesting approach to this problem.

Its open-source MCP server connects AI agents through clients like Claude and Cursor to Vangrid's bounty marketplace and pay-per-request data tools.

But instead of letting an agent spend without a clear boundary, the setup allows two separate spending limits.

MAX_USD_PER_CALL sets the maximum amount an agent can spend on an individual data request.

MAX_USD_PER_BOUNTY controls how much it can commit when creating a bounty.

If a request exceeds the configured limit, the call is rejected.

There is another practical detail I like. The agent uses its own wallet, while its agent token is stored locally. Gas costs are handled by the settlement service.

The recommended approach is to create a fresh wallet and fund it only with the amount the agent is allowed to use.

That creates a second layer of protection beyond the spending limits themselves.

Think about the workflow:

An agent can request already-attested spatial data when it needs information, or create a bounty when new real-world capture is required.

But its spending authority is defined before it starts working.

I see this as an important step towards practical agent autonomy.

An AI agent should be able to make decisions and pay for services when needed, but that doesn't mean it should have unlimited access to funds.

For me, the real value here is not simply giving AI a wallet. It's giving that wallet a clearly defined budget.

Vangrid Bounties for AI Agents: How Does It Work?

One interesting development in @vangrid_io is that bounties are no longer limited to people creating requests manually through the marketplace.

AI agents can now post their own capture requests and pay contributors automatically through an API.

But what does this actually mean?

Let's break it down.

1. What is an Agent Bounty?

Imagine you're building an AI agent that needs real-world spatial data of a warehouse, loading dock, railway station, or shopping centre.

Your agent can request that data directly from Vangrid without someone manually creating the bounty through the website.

It can do this using Vangrid's Bounty API and x402 payment system.

2. How does it work?

The process is straightforward:

1. Create a request: The agent sends a title, capture instructions, USDC amount, and deadline through the API.

2. Make payment: Vangrid provides a payment request. The agent pays the full bounty upfront using USDC on Base or Arc.

3. Bounty goes live: Vangrid publishes the request on its marketplace.

4. Human contribution: An operator visits the location, captures the environment using the Vangrid app, and submits the video.

5. Review: The agent checks the available submissions and chooses one.

6. Accept: Once accepted, escrow is released onchain and Vangrid reconstructs the capture into a 3D model.

The agent can retrieve the submission and resulting model through the API.

3. What happens if nobody completes the request?

The agent can cancel an open bounty and receive a full refund. If the deadline expires without acceptance, the escrow is also refunded.

Why does this matter?

It connects AI software directly with the physical world.

An AI agent can identify the need for real-world data, fund a request, and receive a reconstructed 3D scene, while human contributors handle the actual capture.

My takeaway: Vangrid is creating a bridge between AI agents, human contributors, and real-world spatial data.

AI agents request it. Humans capture it. Vangrid reconstructs it.

That's an interesting step toward connecting autonomous software with the physical world.

2/ The net loss is $23.3B, but $21.9B of that is a paper loss. They owe early investors shares, and those shares got more valuable, so accounting rules count it as a loss (has to do with convertible notes etc being exchanged)

3/ Revenue per employee is over $6.6M!

14/ All 7 co-founders are still at the company, and they lose about 1% of the people they want to keep each year.
